message:
QUESTION:
How much did the SMS reminder scheme reduce missed appointments (no-shows) at the GP practice, and what is it worth per quarter?

DATA:
GP practice. From 1 January, an SMS reminder is sent two days before every appointment booked more than 3 days in advance. Appointments booked 3 days ahead or less get no reminder.

| Period | Booking lead time | Appointments | No-shows |
| Oct-Dec (before) | More than 3 days ahead | 2,400 | 312 |
| Oct-Dec (before) | 3 days or less | 3,600 | 228 |
| Jan-Mar (after) | More than 3 days ahead (SMS sent) | 3,200 | 160 |
| Jan-Mar (after) | 3 days or less (no SMS) | 3,200 | 288 |

Totals: before, 6,000 appointments and 540 no-shows; after, 6,400 appointments and 448 no-shows.

Operations log: on 3 days in November the practice phone system failed, so patients could not call to cancel or rebook. The practice attributes 120 of the before-period no-shows in the 'more than 3 days ahead' group to those 3 days. No other disruptions occurred in either period.

Cost per SMS: 4p. The practice estimates that each no-show costs £30 in wasted clinician time.

<analysis>
# SMS reminders: effect on missed appointments

## Summary

**Among appointments that received a reminder**, the no-show rate fell by an estimated **3.0 to 5.7 percentage points**. That is about **96 to 181 fewer no-shows per quarter** in the reminded group, worth **£2,900 to £5,400 gross**, or **about £2,750 to £5,300 net** after the £128 SMS cost.

**Practice-wide**, the saving is less certain. Reminders may free up slots that are rebooked at short notice and then missed. If that happens on a large scale, the practice-wide benefit falls to **roughly zero**, and a small net loss cannot be ruled out. On the more plausible readings, the practice-wide saving matches the reminded-group figures above.

The two reminded-group figures are **estimates resting on different assumptions**. They are not a guaranteed floor and ceiling.

**Recommendation: continue the scheme.** The case does not depend on the scheme paying off in every scenario. It costs £128 a quarter. On plausible readings it returns 20 to 40 times that. The least favourable reading is close to break-even rather than a large loss. One quarter of checking what happened to cancelled slots would show where in the range the true effect lies.

## Data and adjustments

Since 1 January, the practice has sent an SMS two days before every appointment booked more than 3 days ahead. Shorter-notice appointments get no reminder. This gives a reminded group and an un-reminded comparison group in the same quarter. I compare October–December (before) with January–March (after).

| Group | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Booked >3 days ahead (reminded from Jan) | 312 / 2,400 = 13.0% | 160 / 3,200 = 5.0% | −8.0 pts |
| … excluding phone-outage no-shows | 192 / 2,400 = 8.0% | 5.0% | **−3.0 pts** |
| Booked ≤3 days ahead (never reminded) | 228 / 3,600 = 6.3% | 288 / 3,200 = 9.0% | **+2.7 pts** |
| All appointments, excluding outage | 420 / 6,000 = 7.0% | 448 / 6,400 = 7.0% | 0.0 pts |

**Phone outage.** The practice attributes 120 of the before-period no-shows in the >3-day group to three days in November when patients could not call to cancel. These were not normal no-shows, so I removed them. That gives an adjusted baseline of 8.0% rather than 13.0% for the reminded group. The 120 is the practice's own estimate. Its effect on the results is assessed below.

**Why the overall figures can't answer the question.** Excluding the outage, the practice-wide no-show rate was 7.0% in both quarters. That flat total fits two different stories:
- The reminders worked, and a seasonal rise in no-shows offset the gain.
- The reminders mainly moved no-shows from long-lead to short-notice appointments.

The overall rate cannot tell these apart. The booking mix also shifted: long-lead bookings rose from 40% to 50% of appointments. The comparison therefore has to be made within lead-time groups. Each group has at least 2,400 appointments, so splitting the data costs little precision.

## Estimated effect within the reminded group

- **Before/after estimate: 3.0 points** (95% CI roughly 1.7 to 4.3). This assumes that, without reminders, the long-lead rate would have stayed at its adjusted 8.0%.
- **Difference-in-differences estimate: 5.7 points** (95% CI roughly 3.8 to 7.5). This assumes that whatever raised short-notice no-shows by 2.7 points would have raised long-lead no-shows by the same amount. Winter illness is one possible cause.

Both estimates are clearly distinguishable from zero on sampling grounds. The confidence intervals treat the 120 outage figure as exact, so they understate the total uncertainty.

**Sensitivity to the outage estimate.** The lower estimate depends heavily on this adjustment:

| Outage no-shows assumed | Before/after | Difference-in-differences |
|---|---|---|
| 80 | 4.7 pts | 7.3 pts |
| 120 (practice estimate) | 3.0 pts | 5.7 pts |
| 160 | 1.3 pts | 4.0 pts |

It is also unclear whether the 120 is the *excess* caused by the outage or *all* no-shows on those days. If it is all of them, about 10 would have happened anyway, at the normal rate of roughly 3 a day in this group. That would raise the before/after estimate slightly, to about 3.4 points.

**Assumptions behind each estimate.**
- *Before/after* ignores seasonality. It is also affected by the 33% rise in long-lead bookings (2,400 to 3,200). If the extra bookings involved different patients or appointment types, part of the change could reflect who was booked rather than the reminder.
- *Difference-in-differences* assumes the two groups would have followed the same trend without the scheme. The booking-mix shift weakens this assumption. Short-notice bookings fell from 3,600 to 3,200. If patients who used to book at short notice moved into advance booking, the remaining short-notice group may have changed in make-up, for example towards more urgent or less predictable cases. That could raise its no-show rate regardless of season. In that case the 2.7-point rise overstates the seasonal effect, and so does the 5.7-point estimate.

## Practice-wide effect: the spillover question

Reminders may prompt patients to cancel. If the freed slots are rebooked at short notice by patients who miss them more often, the scheme itself causes some of the short-notice rise. The practice-wide saving is then the reduction in the reminded group *minus* those extra short-notice no-shows. This applies to both estimates.

| Reading of the short-notice rise | No-shows avoided practice-wide per quarter | Net value per quarter |
|---|---|---|
| Entirely seasonal, affecting both groups equally (difference-in-differences) | ~181 | ~£5,300 |
| Unrelated cause affecting only short-notice bookings (before/after) | ~96 | ~£2,750 |
| Entirely spillover caused by the scheme (least favourable) | ~11 | ~£200 |

**The least favourable reading is effectively break-even.** Its figure of about 11 no-shows comes from subtracting two estimates, each with sampling error of roughly ±40 no-shows. The 95% interval runs from about 48 more no-shows to about 70 fewer, or roughly −£1,600 to +£2,000 net per quarter. The result is also sensitive to the outage figure. If the outage accounted for 160 no-shows rather than 120, this reading gives about 43 *more* no-shows practice-wide (about −£1,400 net). So in this scenario the scheme's practice-wide effect is close to zero, and a modest loss cannot be excluded.

**How likely is full spillover?** The data are somewhat reassuring but not conclusive. Short-notice bookings *fell* from 3,600 to 3,200. Large-scale rebooking of freed slots would tend to push that number up. However, total bookings rose, and short-notice volume may have fallen for other reasons. Freed slots could therefore still have been rebooked. This reading should be treated as unlikely but possible until the cancelled-slot check is done (Recommendation 2).

## Value per quarter

These figures assume no spillover. They apply to the roughly 3,200 reminded appointments per quarter, not to all 6,400.

| | Before/after (3.0 pts) | Difference-in-differences (5.7 pts) |
|---|---|---|
| No-shows avoided in reminded group | ~96 | ~181 |
| Value at £30 each | £2,880 | £5,440 |
| SMS cost (3,200 × 4p)¹ | £128 | £128 |
| **Net benefit per quarter** | **~£2,750** | **~£5,300** |
| Cost per no-show avoided | ~£1.33 | ~£0.71 |
| Return on SMS spend | ~22× | ~42× |

¹ Reminders also go to appointments that are later cancelled, and these may not be in the 3,200 count. Even if 20% more messages were sent, the extra cost would be about £26 a quarter, which does not affect any conclusion.

**What "worth" means here.** The £30 is the practice's estimate of clinician time wasted per no-show. It is not cash saved. If some no-show slots are already partly used, for example by walk-ins or overrunning clinics, the true value per avoided no-show is lower. On the plausible readings this does not change the conclusion: the value per no-show would have to fall below about £1.33 before the scheme stopped covering its cost.

Annual figures (roughly £11,000 to £21,000 net on the plausible readings) should be treated with caution until a full year of data covers all seasons.

## Recommendations

1. **Continue the scheme.** On plausible readings it returns 20 to 40 times its £128 quarterly cost. In the least favourable reading, where all of the short-notice rise is displacement caused by the scheme, the practice-wide effect is roughly break-even. Given that limited downside, the large likely upside, and how cheaply the open question can be settled, continuing is the right call.
2. **Check what happened to cancelled slots.** For January–March, count:
   - the appointments cancelled after a reminder,
   - how many of those slots were rebooked at short notice,
   - the no-show rate of those rebookings.

   This is the most useful single check. It shows where in the range the practice-wide effect lies.
3. **Clarify the outage figure.** Confirm whether the 120 counts excess no-shows or all no-shows linked to the outage, and how it was estimated. The lower estimate moves by more than a point for every 40 no-shows of error.
4. **Check the make-up of the short-notice group.** Compare appointment types and patient characteristics in short-notice bookings before and after January. This tests whether the shift in booking mix, rather than season, drove part of the 2.7-point rise.
5. **Trial day-before reminders for 2–3-day bookings** on some days or clinics only. That provides a concurrent comparison group rather than another before/after comparison.
6. **Report monthly no-show rates split by booking lead time,** and log any operational disruptions so they can be excluded. Review the scheme after a full year, comparing January–March against the same quarter next year to remove seasonal effects.
</analysis>

Produce the final version of this analysis.
